# Preface {-}

This project is the second assignment of the ‘Data Science: Capstone’ course (PH125.9x), offered by edX HarvardX. The project aims to build and compare different Handwritten Character Recognition (HCR) models, applying different Machine Learning (ML) techniques, and using a publicly available dataset for training and validation.

# Overview and Executive Summary {#intro}

As noted in the article [Handwritten Character Recognition: A Comprehensive Survey](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/10420981), Handwritten Character Recognition (HCR) plays a vital role in numerous domains, including document digitization, automatic text recognition, signature verification, and postal automation. Over the years, HCR has advanced significantly, driven by the growing demand for accurate, efficient recognition systems [@AAASM_SICI10420981].

## Project Description
::: {.noteblock data-latex=""}
All the source files for *this Project* are available in the *Project*’s [GitHub repository](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own)[@edx.Capstone_CYO].
:::

In this project, we will develop and explore several HCR Multiclass Classifier (MCC) models, based on popular ML algorithms that convert handwritten alphanumeric symbols into a digital, machine-readable form.

We will start with [Shallow Learning (SL)](https://soulpageit.com/ai-glossary/shallow-learning-explained/) models, using [k-Nearest Neighbors (kNN)](https://rafalab.dfci.harvard.edu/dsbook-part-2/ml/resampling-methods.html#sec-knn-cv-intro) and [Random Forest (RF)](https://rafalab.dfci.harvard.edu/dsbook-part-2/ml/algorithms.html#sec-random-forests) methods. These models development and evaluation are described in detail below in Sections [kNN+PCA MCC Model] and [Random Forest (RF) MCC Model] of *this Report*, respectively.

Next, we will try [Deep Learning (DL)](https://soulpageit.com/ai-glossary/deep-learning-explained/) models, including [Dense Neural Network (DNN)](https://smltar.com/dldnn) and, finally, [Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)](https://smltar.com/dlcnn#what-are-cnns) models, as recent research shows that DL performs better at image recognition — the task addressed by *this Project*.

A more detailed explanation of *Deep Learning* versus *Shallow Learning* can be found in the chapter [Machine Learning Methods from Shallow Learning to Deep Learning](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-031-69499-8_1?status=info&saved-doi=10.1007%2F978-3-031-69499-8_1) of the book [Shallow Learning vs. Deep Learning: A Practical Guide for Machine Learning Solutions](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-031-69499-8?status=info&saved-doi=10.1007%2F978-3-031-69499-8) by editors Ömer Faruk Ertuğrul, Josep M. Guerrero, and Musa Yilmaz[@Akinci2024].

The ***DNN-Based*** models are as follows:

* ***Dense Neural Network-Based Basic (DNNB) MCC Model:*** described in Section [DNN-Based Basic (DNNB) MCC Model];
* ***Tuned DNN-Based MCC Model:*** described in Section [Tuned DNN-Based (TDNN) MCC Model].

The last models we will build and explore, the ***CNN-Based*** models, are as follows:

* ***CNN-Based Basic MCC Model:*** described in Section [CNN-Based Basic (CNNB) MCC Model];
* ***Tuned CNN-Based MCC Model:*** described in Section [Tuned CNN-Based (TCNN) MCC Model].

Finally, we will conduct a final test of the best model we have developed, using a specially designated dataset, and see what we will achieve.

## Environment Setup
::: {.noteblock data-latex=""}
The environment setup instructions are provided in the [Prerequisites & Setup](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/README.md#prerequisites--setup) Section of the [README](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/README.md) document on [GitHub](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own).
:::

The environment setup configures an `R`-based machine learning environment with *Python* integration, required to build the *Deep Learning* models.

The installation follows a *4-step* process by sequentially running the following scripts:

* [1.install-reticulate&miniconda.R](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/support-scripts/setup-env/1.install-reticulate&miniconda.R):
  1. *Installs [reticulate](https://rstudio.github.io/reticulate/articles/package.html):* Configures the primary `R` package, the [R Interface to Python](https://rstudio.github.io/reticulate/); 
  2. *Installs [Miniconda](https://continuumio-docs.readthedocs-hosted.com/miniconda/)* to manage Python virtual environments cleanly without conflicting with system Python installations. 


::: { #env_setup.step2 .sidebar}
* [2.install-tensorflow.R](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/support-scripts/setup-env/2.install-tensorflow.R): 
  1. **Installs the [R TensorFlow interface](https://github.com/rstudio/tensorflow):** Loads the TensorFlow R bindings;
  2. **Configures Backend Engine:** Uses reticulate to set up a dedicated *Python virtual/conda environment* and [installs the core C++/Python TensorFlow package](https://tensorflow.rstudio.com/install/) inside it.

:::

* [3.install-keras3.R](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/support-scripts/setup-env/3.install-keras3.R):
  1.  **Installs the Keras3 package:** Installs the [R Interface for Keras3](https://rstudio.r-universe.dev/keras3).
  2. **Binds High-Level Neural Network APIs:** Integrates `Keras` on top of the backend installed in [step 2](#env_setup.step2) to enable building and training *Deep Learning* models in `R`.  

* [4,install-kerastuner.R](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/support-scripts/setup-env/4.install-kerastuner.R): Installs ***Hyperparameter Tuning Tools***, including [R interface to Keras Tuner](https://eagerai.github.io/kerastuneR/). Configures the [KerasTuner](https://keras.io/keras_tuner/) in `R` to automate [Hyperparameter Optimization](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/deep-learning/keras-tuner-for-hyperparameter-optimization/) (*search space*, *trial execution*, and *model evaluation*).

### Batch Execution & Cleanup Scripts

As stated in the [Prerequisites & Setup](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/README.md#prerequisites--setup) Section of the [README](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/README.md) document on [GitHub](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own), on *Windows OS*, all 4 steps of the setup process described above can be completed automatically by launching the [__setup-env.cmd](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/support-scripts/setup-env/__setup-env.cmd) *Windows command script* in *PowerShell* or *Command Prompt*.

The script [__uninstall-all.R](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/support-scripts/setup-env/__uninstall-all.R) cleans up the environment by wiping installed packages, *Conda environments*, and *Python bindings*.

## Running the Project

Once the system environment is fully configured, if you have enough time to execute all the scripts and automatically generate *this report* upon their completion in a single session, the easiest approach is to run the [__run-all.R](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/support-scripts/__run-all.R) script.

This script serves as a starting point for running the project execution pipeline that culminates in a *PDF report*. It coordinates the process by sequentially executing two main R scripts, ensuring the script files exist, and outputs detailed execution logs to both the console and log files.

The first script it launches, [index.R](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/index.R),  is the entry point to the project's execution pipeline and the main script that runs all the other execution scripts sequentially. 

The second (and last) script it runs, [__rmd.render.R](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/support-scripts/__rmd.render.R), renders *this Report*. 

::: {.warningblock data-latex=""}
Some scripts may take a long time when executed on their first run. In particular, the longest run on the *author's laptop* (for technical specifications, see [Appendix C](#appndx_c)) was the first run of the [2.cnn-mcc.lr-tuner.R](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/models/cnn/mcc/tuner/2.cnn-mcc.lr-tuner.R) script (for fine-tuning the *CNN-based MCC* model) and took about **17 hours**.
:::

The other long-running scripts are as follows:

- For tuning and retraining the best (and *final*) *CNN-based MCC* model: 

	- [1.cnn-mcc.arch-tuner.R](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/models/cnn/mcc/tuner/1.cnn-mcc.arch-tuner.R) (took more than **6 hours** on the author's laptop);
	- [3.tcnn-mcc.final.retrain.R](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/models/cnn/mcc/tuner/3.tcnn-mcc.final.retrain.R) (took around **6.5 hours**);

:::

### The Main `R` Script

The [index.R](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/index.R) script serves as the main orchestrator and *entry point* for *this Project*, focused on [Multi-Class Classification (MCC)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiclass_classification) models applied to the [Kaggle Handwritten Character Image Dataset](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/vaibhao/handwritten-characters) (which uses [EMNIST data](https://www.tensorflow.org/datasets/catalog/emnist) for Alphabets and Digits).
Below is a detailed description of the script's structure, workflow, and core components.

::: {.noteblock data-latex=""}
During execution, this script runs several support scripts located in the [support-scripts](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/tree/main/r/support-scripts) folder. 
[Appendix B](#appndx_b) of *this Report* describes most of them.
:::

#### Setup & Initialization

The [Workspace Setup](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/index.R#L5-L160) Section of the [index.R](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/index.R) code configures and initializes the *Global Environment* for the current `R` session, as well as downloads, prepares, and preprocesses the *project’s datasets*.

::: {.importantblock data-latex=""}
Code in this Section \underline{must run at the very beginning} of every _`R` session_ **\underline{before any other script executes}**.
:::

The code in *this Section* first calls the [r-global.path.R](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r-global.path.R) script (see [Appendix B](#appndx_b.r_global.path) for details) to initialize the global variables for *this Project*’s essential `R` scripts directory paths.

Next, in the [Project Environment Setup](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/index.R#L10-L20) subsection, it executes the [setup.R](#appndx_b.setup) script, which installs the full set of required packages (those not yet installed), loads the required libraries, and completes the remaining initialization.


The remaining operations (carried out in the [Preparing Input Data](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/index.R#L21-L160) subsection) relate to downloading and preparing the *project datasets*.

#### Downloading & Preprocessing Input Datasets

The code in the [Preparing Input Data](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/index.R#L21-L160) subsection of the [Workspace Setup](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/index.R#L5-L160) section downloads and prepares the *project datasets* in the following order:

1. In the [Download the Kaggle Dataset](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/index.R#L22-L32) subsection, it runs the [ds.kaggle.download.R](#appndx_b.ds.kaggle.download) script to retrieve the [Kaggle dataset](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/vaibhao/handwritten-characters).
2. In the [Prepare Training Set](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/index.R#L33-L109) subsection, the script prepares the *training datasets* by executing dedicated auxiliary scripts in the following order:
    1. In the [Training Set: Load Raw Image Data](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/index.R#L38-L58) subsection, it runs the [load-raw-image-data.R](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/support-scripts/load-raw-image-data.R) script to load the *raw image data* of the *Training Set*.
    2. In the [Training Set: Prepare Standardized Binary Image Data](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/index.R#L59-L99) subsection, it runs the [raw-img.dat2std_bin.R](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/support-scripts/raw-img.dat2std_bin.R) script to *standardize and binarize* the raw image data for the *Training Set*.
    3. In the [Prepare Training Datasets](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/index.R#L100-L109) subsection, it runs the [prepare-training-set.R](#appndx_b.prepare_training_set) script to split the data of the *Training Set* and prepare *ready to use* datasets for training the *Handwritten Character Recognition (HCR)* models.
3. In the [Prepare Final Test Set](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/index.R#L110-L160) subsection, the script prepares the *final test datasets* by executing dedicated auxiliary scripts in the following order:
    1. In the [Final Test Set: Load Raw Image Data](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/index.R#L114-L132) subsection, it runs the [load-raw-image-data.R](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/support-scripts/load-raw-image-data.R) script to load the *raw image data* of the *Validation Set*.
    2. In the [Final Test Set: Prepare Standardized Binary Image Data](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/index.R#L133-L160) subsection, it runs the [raw-img.dat2std_bin.R](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/support-scripts/raw-img.dat2std_bin.R) script to *standardize and binarize* the raw image data for the *Final Test Set*.

#### Machine Learning Model Pipelines

The [ML Models Development](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/index.R#L161-L1066) section implements, tunes, trains, and evaluates a comprehensive benchmarking pipeline for the 39-class Handwritten Character Recognition (HCR) system.

The workflow systematically develops and tests four distinct machine learning architectures, logs evaluation metrics in a comparative results table, and concludes with an in-depth error analysis of common misclassifications.

Additionally, for each model, it generates a visual representation of the following metrics:

* [ROC curves](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/machine-learning/roc-curves-for-multiclass-classification-in-r/);
* [Confusion Matrix](https://rafalab.dfci.harvard.edu/dsbook-part-2/ml/evaluation-metrics.html#the-confusion-matrix);
* **A custom metric:** *Per-Class Accuracy (PCA)* (calculated by the user-defined helper function [MCClassifier.accuracy.by_class](#func.MCClassifier.accuracy.by_class) described in section [Models Helper / Calculating PCA & Constructing Bar Chart](#appndx_a.mh.calc_pca.bar_chart) of [Appendix A](#appndx_a)).

##### [Shallow Learning (SL)](https://soulpageit.com/ai-glossary/shallow-learning-explained/) Models
\

The *SL models* are implemented in the following sections of the script:

- The [kNN+PCA MCC Model](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/index.R#L162-L269) script section implements a model that combines [Principal Component Analysis (PCA)](https://rafalab.dfci.harvard.edu/dsbook-part-2/highdim/dimension-reduction.html#sec-pca) (for data preprocessing) and [k-Nearest Neighbors (kNN)](https://rafalab.dfci.harvard.edu/dsbook-part-2/ml/resampling-methods.html#sec-knn-cv-intro). The implementation, which uses the [caret::train](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/caret/refman/caret.html#train) function, is described in detail in the [kNN+PCA MCC Model] section of *this Report*.   
- The [Random Forest (RF) MCC Model](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/index.R#L270-L381) script section implements the [Random Forest (RF)](https://rafalab.dfci.harvard.edu/dsbook-part-2/ml/algorithms.html#sec-random-forests) algorithm. The implementation, which uses the [caret::train](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/caret/refman/caret.html#train) function, is described in detail in the [Random Forest (RF) MCC Model] section of *this Report*.

\newpage

##### [Deep Learning (DL)](https://soulpageit.com/ai-glossary/deep-learning-explained/) Models
\

The *DL models* are implemented in the following sections of the script:

- The [DNN-Based MCC Model](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/index.R#L382-L667) script section implements the [Dense Neural Network (DNN)](https://liora.io/en/dense-neural-networks-understanding-their-structure-and-function) architecture. The implementation, described in detail in the [Dense Neural Network Based Multiclass Classifier (DNN-Based MCC) Models] section of *this Report*, includes the following two models:
  * *DNN-Based Basic (DNNB) MCC* implemented by the script subsection [DNN-Based Basic MCC Model](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/index.R#L383-L519) and described in subsection [DNN-Based Basic (DNNB) MCC Model];
  * *Fine-Tuned DNN (TDNN) MCC* implemented by the script subsection [DNN-Based MCC Model Tuning](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/index.R#L520-L667) and described in subsection [Tuned DNN-Based (TDNN) MCC Model].

- The [CNN-based MCC Model](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/index.R#L668-L1066) script section implements the [Couvolutional Neural Network (CNN)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convolutional_neural_network) architecture. The implementation, described in detail in the [Convolutional Neural Network Based (CNN) MCC Models] section of *this Report*, includes the following two models:

  * *CNN-Based Basic (CNNB) MCC* implemented by the script subsection [CNN-Based Basic MCC Model](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/index.R#L671-L812) and described in subsection [CNN-Based Basic (CNNB) MCC Model];
  * *Fine-Tuned CNN (TCNN) MCC* implemented by the script subsection [CNN-Based MCC Model Tuning](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/index.R#L813-L1066) and described in subsection [Tuned CNN-Based (TCNN) MCC Model].


##### The *Final Test* of the Best Model

The latest model we developed (described below in section [Tuned CNN-Based (TCNN) MCC Model]) achieves the highest accuracy (the metric is used to assess performance). So we apply the *Final Test* to this model using the [Validation portion](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/vaibhao/handwritten-characters?select=Validation) of the *Kaggle dataset*.

The *Final Test* is performed by the [4.tcnn-mcc.final-test.R](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/models/cnn/mcc/tuner/4.tcnn-mcc.final-test.R) script invoked from the [CNN-Based MCC Model Tuning / Run Scripts](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/index.R#L885) section of the *main script*. The [TCNN MCC: Final Test] section below provides the details.

###### The Most Frequent Error Results Review 

The script section [Reviewing the Most Frequent Error Results](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/index.R#L988-L1066) implements the recognition error analysis phase, which pinpoints the most confusing characters that cause the poorest recognition performance.
 
Finally, it visualizes several image examples of such characters, along with information about which characters they were confused with.

The [The Most Confusing Characters for Recognition] section below provides the details and visualizations of the confused character examples.

## Datasets Overview

```{r intro.datasets-overview$open-log, include=FALSE}
stopifnot(file.exists(train.img.std_bin.ls.nested.file,
                      final_test.img.std_bin.ls.nested.file))
```

The project uses the [HandWritten_Character Dataset](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/vaibhao/handwritten-characters)  downloaded from [Kaggle](https://www.kaggle.com).As mentioned in the section [Downloading & Preprocessing Input Datasets] above, the dedicated script [ds.kaggle.download.R](#appndx_b.ds.kaggle.download) (described below in [Appendix B](#appndx_b)) is used for that purpose. The result of its execution is a folder structure (identical to one shown on the dataset's webpage) containing the raw image data, as shown below:

```{r intro.datasets-overview.downloading@dir_tree, echo=FALSE, output.size="small"}

writeLines("*** Dataset Raw Data Local Directory Structure ***")
dir_tree(raw_data.chars.dir, type = 'directory')
```

\newpage

### Preprocessing Raw Image Data

To make the downloaded raw image data ready for use in the *Machine Learning Model Pipelines*, it must be properly preprocessed.
The raw data processing starts by loading it from its storage files into `R` objects for further transformation.

As mentioned in the [Downloading & Preprocessing Input Datasets] section above, this feature is implemented in the [load-raw-image-data.R](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/support-scripts/load-raw-image-data.R) script, [which calls](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/support-scripts/load-raw-image-data.R#L16) a dedicated custom helper function, [load_image.list](#func.load_image.list), described below in [Appendix A](#appndx_a), to perform the operation. 

The [Kaggle dataset](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/vaibhao/handwritten-characters) description provided on the *landing page* describes the *context* of the dataset as follows:

::: {.accentquote data-latex=""}
1. Used *EMNIST* data for Alphabets and Digits.
2. Transformed the Data using some image processing techniques and convert it to 32,32 pixel black and white images.
3. Created the Data set for special character ( @, #, $, & )
3. Merged the Categories to avoid the misclassification
4. Total 39 Categories in Train and Validation set

:::

However, although the [dataset author](https://www.kaggle.com/vaibhao) claims that the images were transformed into 32x32-pixel grayscale images, a quick analysis of the raw data showed that at least some images have different sizes. 

So the author of *this Report* has decided to standardize the images by resizing them to the smallest image size found in the dataset.

This functionality has been implemented in the [raw-img.dat2std_bin.R](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/support-scripts/raw-img.dat2std_bin.R) support script described below in [Appendix B: Support Scripts].

First, the [Define the Standard Image Size Geometry](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/support-scripts/raw-img.dat2std_bin.R#L30-L73) section of the script implements the *Dynamic Geometry Determination* feature, which determines the geometry parameters for the image standardization..

Execution of this section yields the [following result](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/support-scripts/raw-img.dat2std_bin.R#L70):

```{r intro.datasets-overview@uniform-size, echo=FALSE}
put_log("The geometry for standardizing images to a uniform size, 
based on the smallest existing image in the Training Set, is as follows: 
%1", ds.img_min.geometry)
```

Meaning that the smallest image size is 28x28 pixels.

\newpage

We can use the following code snippet to prepare a few sample images, both 28x28 and 32x32 pixels in size, for visual presentation:

```{r intro.ds-overview@img.diff-size$data, output.size="footnotesize" }
print(paste("Kaggle Dataset Root Directory:", img.train_root.dir))

chr_set <- c('#', '$', '&', '@', 
             '1', 'L', 'I', 'J',
             '6', 'B', 'D', '5',
             '9', 'G', 'Q', 'S' )

img.files <- sapply(chr_set, function(chr) {
  dir_path <- file.path(img.train_root.dir, chr)
  file.path(dir_path, dir(dir_path)[1])
  
})

img.annotation <- sapply(seq_len(length(img.files)), function(i){
  img <- magick::image_read(img.files[i])
  img.dat <- image_data(img)
  img.dim <- dim(img.dat)
  
  img.size <- paste0(img.dim[2], 'x', img.dim[3], 'px')
#   print_log("`%1` character Image size is:
# %2", chr_set[i], img.size)
  
  paste0(chr_set[i],": ", img.size)
})

img.dat <- data.frame(file = img.files,
                      annotation = img.annotation)

print(img.dat$annotation)
```

Figure \@ref(fig:intro-ds-overview-img-diff-size-sample) below shows what these images look like.

```{r intro-ds-overview-img-diff-size-sample, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Example images, both 28x28 and 32x32 pixels."}
print.image_grid(img.dat,
                 # font.size = 20,
                 # image.scale = "50",
                 geometry = '100x',
                 tile = '4x4'
                 )
```

\newpage

Also, given the linear nature of the black-and-white character images in the dataset, meaning halftones play no significant role, it seems appropriate to perform image binarization, as explained in [Section 21.3 Matrix Operations in R / Binarize the data](https://rafalab.dfci.harvard.edu/dsbook-part-2/highdim/matrices-in-R.html#binarize-the-data) of the *Course Textbook (New Edition)*[@IDS2_21.5_BD].


```{r intro.ds-overview@img.diff-size$hist }
hist.grobs <- lapply(chr_set, function(chr) {
  dir_path <- file.path(img.train_root.dir, chr)
  file <- file.path(dir_path, dir(dir_path)[1])

  img <- image_read(file)
  img.mx <- magick_img2matrix(img)
  img.df <- data.frame(pi <- as.vector(img.mx))
  h.title <- paste("Character", chr)
  
  ggplot(img.df, aes(x = pi)) +
    geom_histogram(bins = 30,
                   fill = "steelblue",
                   colour = "white") +
    labs(title = h.title,
         x = "Intensity",
         y = "Frequency") +
    theme_minimal()
})

marrangeGrob(grobs = hist.grobs[1:6], ncol = 3, nrow = 2,  top = NULL, bottom = NULL)
marrangeGrob(hist.grobs[7:16], ncol = 3, nrow = 3, top = NULL, bottom = NULL, padding = unit(0, "line"))

```

#### Standardizing & Binarizing the Image Data

As already mentioned above in the [Downloading & Preprocessing Input Datasets] section, the *raw image data* undergoes preprocessing via the [raw-img.dat2std_bin.R](#appndx_b.raw_img.dat2std_bin) script (described below in [Appendix B](#appndx_b)), which includes *resizing the images to a uniform dimension* (`28x28` in our case) and *binarizing* them.

Additionally, the images are trimmed during preprocessing to remove noninformative spatial data from their edges.

The task runs only once. By the end of execution, it caches the results in a backup file on the local disk. On follow-up calls, it first checks whether the cache exists. If found, it just shows a warning that the results have already been constructed and cached on disk.

::: {.noteblock data-latex=""}
Most of the scripts in *this Project* follow the same pattern: they cache the results on disk upon completion and check the cache on subsequent calls. If found, they either load the results from the cache or merely show a warning message (the former is implemented in the model training scripts; the latter describes how the data processing scripts work).
:::

The result of the script execution consists of the *label list* of the *character classes* and the nested list of *preprocessed character image data*, along with their file paths, grouped by *character class*.

The *label list* is as follows:

```{r intro.ds-overview@label-list, output.size="footnotesize" }
print(train.img.std_bin.ls.nested$label.list)
```

::: { #ds_overview.train.img.std_bin.ls.nested.structure .sidebar }
And the *nested list* of preprocessed character image data of the *Training Set* has the following structure:
```{r intro.ds-overview@train.img.std_bin.ls.nested$structure, output.size="footnotesize" }
str(train.img.std_bin.ls.nested, list.len = 39, max.level = 3)

```
:::

\newpage

The *nested list* of the preprocessed *Validation Set* data (created by the same script and used for the *Final Test* of the *best model* developed in *this Project*) has the following structure:

```{r intro.ds-overview@ft.img.std_bin.ls.nested$structure, output.size="footnotesize" }
str(ft.img.std_bin.ls.nested, list.len = 39, max.level = 3)

```

\newpage

We can immediately observe that both the *Training Set* and *Validation Set* data are considerably imbalanced. Since we are going to use the *accuracy metric* to evaluate our models during the *training stage*, we will need to balance our *training set*.

::: {.noteblock data-latex=""}
We **will not balance** our *Validation Set*, so we can use **\underline{ALL AVAILABLE DATA}** for the *Final Test*.
We will also deliberately refrain from balancing the Train/Test split dataset when retraining the *best final model* we manage to develop, thereby ensuring that the largest possible amount of available data is used for training.
We will keep in mind, though, that plain accuracy is not the most appropriate metric for evaluating test results when dealing with imbalanced datasets. 
As explained in section "4 ASSESSMENT METRICS FOR IMBALANCED LEARNING" of the article [Learning from Imbalanced Data](https://www.academia.edu/86894835/Learning_from_Imbalanced_Data), the *F-Measure metric* and the *Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) Curves* will provide better results when dealing with *imbalanced data*.[@LFID_HHGE5128907]
We will use the [F1-Score metric](https://rafalab.dfci.harvard.edu/dsbook-part-2/ml/evaluation-metrics.html#balanced-accuracy-and-f_1-score) in our *Final Test*. We will also use [ROC curves](https://rafalab.dfci.harvard.edu/dsbook-part-2/ml/evaluation-metrics.html#roc-and-precision-recall-curves) and the [Confusion Matrix](https://rafalab.dfci.harvard.edu/dsbook-part-2/ml/evaluation-metrics.html#the-confusion-matrix) throughout *this Project* to assess our models. Additionally, we will compute accuracy separately for each class (let's call this custom metric *Per-Class Accuracy*, or *PCA* for short). All these additional metrics will give us more insight into our models’ performance, especially when testing on the imbalanced dataset.[@IDS2_27]
:::

```{r intro.ds-overview@train.image-size_28x28}
print(img.min_max.size)
```

Now, let's see what the sample images shown in the Figure \@ref(fig:intro-ds-overview-img-diff-size-sample) above look like after trimming, standardization, and binarization.
For that purpose, we extract the preprocessed image data of the *Training Set* using the following code snippet:
```{r intro.ds-overview@img.same-size$dat, output.size="footnotesize" }
img.sample <- lapply(chr_set, function(chr) {
  img.mx <- train.img.std_bin.ls.nested$img.list[[chr]]$img.list[[1]]
  mode(img.mx) <- "numeric"

  img.array <- array(t(img.mx), dim = c(nrow(img.mx), ncol(img.mx), 1))
  img <- image_read(img.array)
  image_data(img)
})

img.annotation <- sapply(seq_len(length(img.files)), function(i){
  img.dat <- img.sample[[i]]
  img.dim <- dim(img.dat)
  
  img.size <- paste0(img.dim[2], 'x', img.dim[3], 'px')
  paste0(chr_set[i],": ", img.size)
})

img.dat <- data.frame(file = img.files,
                      annotation = img.annotation)

print(img.dat$annotation)
```

Now, we can see that all the sample images are the same size.

Figure \@ref(fig:intro-ds-overview-img-std-bin-sample) below shows what these images look like.

We can't even see any noticeable differences in the sample images after preprocessing, can we? (See Figure \@ref(fig:intro-ds-overview-img-diff-size-sample) above for comparison.)

So, we can be pretty sure these changes will not affect the models' recognition ability.
At the same time, it is quite clear that this preprocessing can significantly speed up the training process and substantially reduce computational resource consumption.

The next step in *image data preprocessing* performed by the code in [Preparing a List of Image Data Matrix Arrays](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/support-scripts/raw-img.dat2std_bin.R#L141-L203) of the script is binding the *image data matrices* in the nested list into a single *array of matrices* for each *character class* for both the *Training Set* and the *Validation Set*. 
```{r intro.datasets-overview@img-dat.mx-array-list$init, include=FALSE}
train.img.std_bin.array.ls <- readRDS(train.img.std_bin.array.ls.file)
final_test.img.std_bin.array.ls <- readRDS(final_test.img.std_bin.array.ls.file)

str.inner_list <- function(i, ls) {
  print_log("$ %1:%2", Y.Labels[i], capture.output(str(ls[[i]])))
}

str.img.std_bin.array.ls <- function(ls, 
                                     .range, 
                                     etc_line = FALSE, 
                                     outer_list = FALSE) {

  if(outer_list)
    str(ls, max.level = 0)
  
  for(i in .range) {
    str.inner_list(i,ls)
  }
  
  if(etc_line) {
    writeLines("
    ...............................................
    ")
  }
}
```

::: {.noteblock data-latex=""}
For the *CNN-based models*, we also need to reshape our datasets to meet the requirements of the [2D convolution layer](https://keras3.posit.co/reference/layer_conv_2d.html) in the [Keras 3](https://keras3.posit.co/) package we use. 

To work with these models, we will reshape the *preprocessed image data* (with shape `28x28`) into a *3D tensor* with shape $(28, 28, 1)$, where the last dimension is for the image *grayscale channel*.  

More information and explanation can be found in [Chapter 4: Deep learning for computer vision](https://s-ai-f.github.io/Computer-vision-keras-R/), *Section 4.2 Introduction to Convolution Neural Networks* of the book [Computer vision with R and keras](https://s-ai-f.github.io/Computer-vision-keras-R/).
:::

#### Preparing the Training Datasets

To use the *Training Set* datasets for training our models. we need to split them into *Train/Test* sets as explained in [Section 29.6 Cross-validation](https://rafalab.dfci.harvard.edu/dsbook-part-2/ml/resampling-methods.html#cross-validation) of the *Course Textbook*. This is done in the [prepare-training-set.R](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/support-scripts/prepare-training-set.R) script.

::: {.noteblock data-latex=""}
The *Validation Set* used in our project plays the role of the *Independent Set* in the terms used in the *Textbook*[@IDS2_29.6]. We can treat it this way because \underline{it is entirely independent} of the *Training Set*, and is used **solely to \underline{evaluate our best model}** at the end of the study.

Also, we split each of our datasets (into the *Train/Test* sets) only once; we do not use the *k-fold cross-validation* (described in [Section 29.6 Cross-validation / K-fold cross-validation](https://rafalab.dfci.harvard.edu/dsbook-part-2/ml/resampling-methods.html#k-fold-cross-validation) of the *Course Textbook*[@IDS2_29.6_KFCV]) explicitly in our scripts because of the restricted time we have for the models’ training, although it is used under the hood in the [caret::train](https://topepo.github.io/caret/model-training-and-tuning.html) function used for the [Shallow Learning Models], i.e., for the [kNN+PCA MCC Model] and [Random Forest (RF) MCC Model].
:::

Before we split our datasets, there is one thing left to do: to train our [Shallow Learning Models] (the [kNN+PCA MCC](#knn_pca_model) and [Random Forest MCC](#rf_model) ones) and the [DNN-Based Basic MCC Model](#dnnb_model), the *training dataset* (let's call it the *Normalized Training Dataset*) needs to be flattened; that is, our *image data matrices* must be coerced into vectors of $x*y$ length (the number of pixels: $28*28 = 784$ in our case). 

This functionality is implemented in the [Preparing Flattened EMNIST-Like Dataset](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/support-scripts/prepare-training-set.R#L8-L52) section of the script, [which calls](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/support-scripts/prepare-training-set.R#L28) the user-defined helper function [img.list2flatten_matrix](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/support-functions/data-helper.R#L557) (defined in the [Data processing](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/support-functions/data-helper.R#L519-L1080) section of the [data-helper.R](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/support-functions/data-helper.R#L557) script) to transform the dataset, consisting of the [nested list of the standardized and binarized data matrices](#ds_overview.train.img.std_bin.ls.nested.structure) we obtained after the very first step of the image data preprocessing described in the [Standardizing & Binarizing the Image Data] section above, into the required format.

Since the result of the transformation is cached on the local disk, we can load the dataset from the backup file:

```{r prep.train_set@ds_flattened$print_backup_flle_name, echo=FALSE}
print_log("The Flattened Training set was cached in the following file:
%1", ds.train.flatten.file)
```
```{r prep.train_set@ds_flattened$init}

ds.train.flattened <- readRDS(ds.train.flatten.file)
```

##### The Train/Test Model-Specific Split Datasets
\

Now, we are ready to split the mostly preprocessed *Training Sets* into the following *training and test subsets*:

- **Flattened Training Dataset** splits for the following *Shallow Learning* and *Deep Learning* DNN-based basic models:

  - ***k-Nearest Neighbors (kNN) MCC*** model (described in Section [kNN+PCA MCC Model]);
  - ***Random Forest (RF) MCC*** model (described in Section [Random Forest (RF) MCC Model]);
  - ***Dense Neural Network Basic (DNNB) MCC*** model (described in Section [DNN-Based Basic (DNNB) MCC Model]).

- **Normalized Training Dataset** splits for *Deep Learning MCC* models (based on Neural Networks: *DNN* and *CNN*):

  - ***Fine-Tuned DNN-Based (TDNN) MCC*** (described in Section [Tuned DNN-Based (TDNN) MCC Model]);
  - ***CNN-Based MCC*** models (described in Section [Convolutional Neural Network Based (CNN) MCC Models]). 

We use two types of split sets (both for *Normalized* and *Flattened* datasets):

- **0.8/0.2 ratio split of the *Train/Test* sets:** (*by default*) for preliminary training and retraining the best models after tuning;  
- **0.1/0.9 ratio split of the *Train/Test* sets:** “lite” *Training Set* to use for tuning the models (due to the time-consuming nature of such operations) and “heavy” *Test Set* to use the maximum amount of available data for testing to achieve more reliable results.

###### Flatten Training Set Splits
\

The feature that creates *balanced split datasets* is implemented in the [prepare-flattened-datasets.R](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/support-scripts/prepare-flattened-datasets.R) script, which invokes the custom helper function [ds.flatten.sample](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/support-functions/data-helper.R#L908) (defined in the [Data processing](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/support-functions/data-helper.R#L519-L1080) section of the [data-helper.R](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/support-functions/data-helper.R#L908) script), which, in fact, performs the actual splitting of the provided data according to the specified proportion.

::: {.noteblock data-latex=""}
This script itself [is invoked](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/support-scripts/prepare-training-set.R#L61) from the [Splitting the Flattened Dataset](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/support-scripts/prepare-training-set.R#L53-L70) section of the [prepare-training-set.R](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/support-scripts/prepare-training-set.R#L61) script, which also implements all other splitting operations listed above in the [The Train/Test Model-Specific Split Datasets] section.
:::

As always, the result of the data processing is cached on the local disk, so we can later load the dataset from the backup file:

```{r ds.flattened.split@print_backup_flle_name, echo=FALSE}
print_log("The Default Flattened Split Set was cached in the following file:
%1", ds.flatten.split.file)
```
```{r ds.flattened.split@init}
stopifnot(file.exists(ds.flatten.split.file))
ds.flattened.split <- readRDS(ds.flatten.split.file)
```

\newpage

The *Default Flattened Split Set* has the following structure:
```{r ds.flattened.split@struct}
str(ds.flattened.split)
```


::: { #func.ds.group_by_class .sidebar }
Now, let's write a function that groups our *split dataset* by *Character Class* to see whether it is properly balanced:  
```{r ds.flattened.split@group_by_class}
ds.group_by_class <- function(x) {
  y <- as.factor(rownames(x))

  data.frame(classID = y) |> 
    group_by(classID) |>
    summarise(n = n())  
}

```
:::

\newpage

So, we can see that this is true for the *training set*:
``` {r ds.flattened.split@train$groupped_by_class, output.size="footnotesize"}
print(ds.group_by_class(ds.flattened.split$train_set$x.train), 
      n = N.classes)
```

\newpage

As well as for the *test set*:
``` {r ds.flattened.split@test$groupped_by_class, output.size="footnotesize"}
print(ds.group_by_class(ds.flattened.split$test_set$x.test), 
      n = N.classes)
```

\newpage

```{r ds.flattened0.1split@print_backup_flle_name, echo=FALSE}
was cached in the following file:

```

###### Normalized Training Set Splits
\

For the *Normalized* dataset, the *Balanced Splitting* feature is implemented in the following subsections of the [Splitting the Training Dataset (Array of Matrices)](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/support-scripts/prepare-training-set.R#L71-L194) section of the [prepare-training-set.R](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/support-scripts/prepare-training-set.R) script:

- **Default Splitting:** implemented in the [Splitting by Default (0.8/0.2 Ratio Train/Test Sets)](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/support-scripts/prepare-training-set.R#L72-L112) subsection;
- **Splitting into a 01/0.9 ratio *Train/Test* Sets:** implemented in the [Splitting into 0.1/0.9 Ratio Train/Test Sets (for the Models' Tuning)](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/support-scripts/prepare-training-set.R#L113-L151) subsection.

Finally, the subsection [Splitting by Default Without Balancing (for the Final Retraining of the Best Model)](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/support-scripts/prepare-training-set.R#L152-L193) implements the *Default Non-Balanced Splitting* feature, which splits the dataset into a 0.8/0.2 ratio *\underline{imbalanced} Train/Test Sets* (for retraining the *Final Best Model* that will be developed at the end of the study).

::: {.noteblock data-latex=""}
All of the *split datasets* listed above in this section are created by the custom helper function [ds.split.img_mx.array](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/support-functions/data-helper.R#L520) (defined in the [Data processing](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/support-functions/data-helper.R#L519-L1080) section of the [data-helper.R](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/support-functions/data-helper.R#L520) script), which is called for each pair of *Train/Test* sets from the corresponding sections of the [prepare-training-set.R](https://github.com/AzKurban-edX-DS/edx.capstone.choose-your-own/blob/main/r/support-scripts/prepare-training-set.R) script.
:::

Again, the result of the data processing is cached on the local disk, so we can later load the dataset from the backup file:

###### Imbalanced Split Dataset for Retraining the *Best Final Model*
\

This split is implemented in the section [Splitting by Default Without Balancing (for the Final Retraining of the Best Model)] of the script by executing the custom helper function [ds.split.img_mx.array] mentioned above (the same one used for any other splits described in the [Normalized Training Set Splits] section) with the argument value `balanced = FALSE`.

As before, we can load our *Default Imbalanced Split Sets* from the cache file:

#### Validation Dataset for the Final Test 
\

For the *Final Test*, we will use the *entire preprocessed* [Validation Set](#validation_set.struct) as described in the section [Standardizing & Binarizing the Image Data] above, without any splitting or sampling.

As previously mentioned, to obtain a more accurate assessment of the results, we will additionally employ the [F1-score](https://rafalab.dfci.harvard.edu/dsbook-part-2/ml/evaluation-metrics.html#balanced-accuracy-and-f_1-score) metric, given that the *validation dataset* exhibits a significant class imbalance.

We can observe this using the *custom helper function* [ds.group_by_class](#func.ds.group_by_class) we defined above in the section [Flatten Training Set Splits]:
``` {r ds.validation_set@groupped_by_class, output.size="footnotesize"}
print(ds.group_by_class(final_test.img.std_bin.array$img_dat.array), 
      n = N.classes)
```
